title: Leadership Lessons From Winston Churchill—The Roaring Lion
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston draws leadership lessons from Winston Churchill's handling of 1940, when Britain faced invasion and even his own cabinet wavered. He frames Churchill through Jim Collins' Good to Great research, where every Level 5 Leader combined fierce professional will with deep humility. Houston then lists the behaviors that showed those traits: giving people hope they did not yet know they had, courage to continue, constant top-down and bottom-up communication, deliberately seeking opposing viewpoints, and visible compassion. The Dunkirk evacuation, in which about 800 civilian boats helped rescue more than 338,000 troops, closes the piece as a lesson in doing what you can when the odds are overwhelming. The essay is short and illustrative rather than rigorous, but it links a historical case to a research-based leadership model.
points: Collins' Level 5 Leaders paired fierce professional will with deep humility, giving credit away and taking responsibility when things went badly.
Churchill built his war cabinet from people who disagreed with him to counter his own bias, an example of humility as a decision-making discipline.
Communicating more in a crisis, across the inner circle, the legislature and the public, was central to his leadership.
Leaders broker in hope, offering people a belief in the future before they know they have it.
The Dunkirk civilian boats show that overwhelming odds do not excuse inaction, since small contributions add up.
quotes: Every single Level 5 Leader had two indispensable qualities that seemed paradoxical—1) Fierce professional will and 2) Deep humility.
They took responsibility when things went badly, and gave away credit when things went well.
Great leaders provide the hope before people even know they have it. This is self-leadership at its best.
Churchill deliberately assembled his war cabinet from people who didn’t see things his way, in an effort to counter his own potential for bias. Now that is inspiring humility.
Most military leaders also agree that it is vital to communicate more during times of crisis, and when your team is working remotely.
Don’t let overwhelming odds prevent you from doing what you can. We are all small boats, but every single boat makes a difference.
